context: The excerpt describes a stochastic error-ellipsoid approach for robot positioning and repeatability. Positioning uncertainty is represented as a spatial distribution of end-effector errors; its covariance determines the ellipsoid’s principal directions and spread. The ellipsoid axes align with directions of greatest variability, which are associated with large sensitivities in the Jacobian (Jacobi) matrix. Nearly spherical ellipsoids indicate similar sensitivity in all directions, while elongated or inclined ellipsoids indicate anisotropic uncertainty and correlated link or drive errors. The study compares compact, medium, and elongated robot configurations. For the FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L, measurements used 25 workspace points and 50 repeated trials per point, with a laser tracker accurate to about 0.01 mm. These repeated samples were used to construct empirical error distributions and covariance matrices, which were compared against model predictions. Monte Carlo analysis was especially important in highly nonlinear or elongated configurations, where analytical and stochastic estimates differed by 7–10%; compact and medium configurations differed by only 1–3%. Thus, probabilistic workspace mapping involves sampling model uncertainties across configurations, estimating covariance/error ellipsoids at workspace locations, and using the resulting map to identify sensitive regions and optimize configurations before assembly or during online condition assessment.

The reported analysis concerns theoretical absolute positioning error over 1,000 randomly generated joint configurations. Vernier remastering produced mean errors of approximately 6.1 mm (motion capture) and 5.6 mm (laser tracker) when zero-offset uncertainty alone was considered, while Bayesian remastering reduced these values to 0.223 mm and 0.183 mm, respectively. When zero-offset uncertainty, unmodeled dynamics, and noise were included, Bayesian remastering yielded mean errors of 1.439 mm and 1.187 mm, with upper-percentile errors below 3 mm. The authors concluded that accuracy improved by at least four-fold across the full workspace. They also found that zero-offset uncertainty accounted for more than 95% of the original Cartesian error after Vernier remastering, but only about 15% of the remaining error after Bayesian remastering.

context: The excerpt reports probabilistic positioning and reliability analysis only for the six-axis FANUC LR Mate 200iD/7L; it does not mention Kinova, UR5, Franka, ABB, or low-cost robot arms, nor does it provide comparative results for those models using error ellipsoids or workspace-accuracy maps. For FANUC, Monte Carlo simulations incorporated stochastic DH-parameter and joint errors, nonlinear direct kinematics, complex permissible regions, correlated errors, and dependence on configuration and trajectory. The analysis produced a reliability map over joint-configuration space, allowing identification of more reliable postures and avoidance of singularity-prone regions. Independent errors in joints 4–6 were associated primarily with orientation errors, while correlated errors in joints 1–3 caused vertical or horizontal displacement of the working point. Correlated errors in DH parameters altered the spatial distribution of posture errors. The robot’s outstretched-arm configurations, particularly those with a large second-joint angle, showed significantly reduced reliability because of increased Jacobian sensitivity. The excerpt also notes that the robot has low independent drive errors, although thermal expansion can produce correlated errors. Monte Carlo was considered useful for complex configuration-dependent reliability assessment, despite high computational cost and the need for importance sampling in rare-event, low-reliability cases.
